title: Wh-questions with who, whom, which, how and whose

sections.title: Who vs Whom
sections.content:
In wh-questions, who is usually the subject and whom is usually the object. Whom is more formal than who:
• Who owns that car? (subject)
• Who did you meet? (object)
Whom is used as a formal alternative to who as object, and also directly after prepositions:
• Whom did you meet? (formal)
• To whom were you talking? (formal)

sections.title: Which vs Who/What
sections.content:
Which is used to refer to people or things when we want to identify one of a group:
• 'Which is your brother?' 'The one next to Luka.' (talking about a photograph)
We can use which instead of who to talk about particular classes of people:
• Which do you think earns more, a teacher or a police officer? (or Who do you think …?)
We usually use which, rather than who or what, in questions before one(s) and of:
• Which one do you think I should choose?
• Which of you would like to go first?

sections.title: Singular and Plural verbs
sections.content:
When we use who or what as subjects, the verb that follows is usually singular, even if a plural answer is expected:
• What is there to see in the town? (expects an answer giving a number of things to see)
However, the verb can be plural in echo questions (see Unit 27E) or when who and what function as complements:
• Who are those people over there?
• What are the consequences of the decision?

sections.title: How or what?
sections.content:
Compare how and what:
• How was the journey? (asking a general opinion)
• What was the journey like? (asking a general opinion)
• How is your brother? (asking about general health)
• What do you like about the job? (asking for details)
• What's it called? (asking about a name)
• How / What about a swim? (making a suggestion)

sections.title: Whose
sections.content:
We can use whose to ask about the person that owns or is responsible for something. Whose can be used either before a verb (as a pronoun):
• Whose are these boots?
or before a noun or noun phrase (as a determiner):
• Whose boots are these?
• She asked me whose coat I was wearing.
In formal contexts we can use a preposition before whose:
• In whose desk was it found? (less formally Whose desk was it found in?)

exercises.question: To ___ should the documents be sent?
exercises.hint: Formal context with preposition before the wh-word.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: whom
Formal context with preposition before the wh-word.

exercises.question: ___ of you is Dr Hansen? I have a message for you.
exercises.hint: Identifying a person from a group.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Which
Use 'which' when choosing from a defined set or group. Use 'who' when asking about any person in general. 'Which of you' is correct because you're identifying one person from a specific, limited group.

exercises.question: A: Is your sister at home? B: What / ___ one do you want to speak to?
exercises.hint: Which one is used when choosing between a limited set.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Which
Which one is used when choosing between a limited set.

exercises.sentence: Who did you speak with him about the problem?
exercises.correction: Who did you speak to about the problem?
acceptable: Who did you speak to about the problem?
Whom did you speak to about the problem?
exercises.hint: Remove 'him' — the question word already represents the person.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Who did you speak to about the problem?
In a wh-question, the question word replaces the person or thing you are asking about. 'Who did you speak to about the problem?' — here 'who' represents the person. Adding 'him' duplicates the reference, which is incorrect.

exercises.question: ___ will captain the team if Zeinab isn't available?
exercises.hint: Subject of the sentence asking about a person.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Who
Use 'who' when asking about the subject (the person performing the action). 'Whom' is used for the object (the person receiving the action). In informal English, 'who' is used for both.

exercises.question: What ___ those cakes made from? (be)
exercises.hint: Who/What as subject usually takes a singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is
Who/What as subject usually takes a singular verb.

exercises.question: Who ___ you for Maths and English?
exercises.hint: Who as subject usually takes a singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: teaches
Who as subject usually takes a singular verb.

exercises.sentence: I don't know where is the nearest bus stop.
exercises.correction: I don't know where the nearest bus stop is.
acceptable: I don't know where the nearest bus stop is.
exercises.hint: Indirect questions use statement word order: where + subject + verb (not inverted).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: where the nearest bus stop is
In direct questions, the verb comes before the subject: 'Where IS the bus stop?' In indirect questions (after 'I don't know', 'Could you tell me', 'I wonder'), use statement word order: 'where the bus stop IS'. This is one of the most common word-order errors in English.

exercises.question: '___ do you like about your new job?' 'It's never boring.'
exercises.explanation:
Answer: What
Use 'what' when asking about things in general or asking for details. Use 'which' when choosing from a defined set. 'What do you like' asks about preferences in general.

exercises.question: '___ about a coffee?' 'I'd love one.'
exercises.hint: Both 'How about' and 'What about' are used for suggestions.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: How or What
Both 'How about' and 'What about' are used for suggestions.

exercises.question: '___'s your boss like?' 'She works us really hard.'

exercises.prompt: Form a question asking about possession:
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Whose laptop is this on the desk?
'Whose' as a determiner before a noun: 'Whose laptop?' not 'Whose is the laptop?' The question structure is: Whose + noun + auxiliary (is/are/was/were) + subject. Compare: 'Whose is this?' (pronoun use, asking about an object already pointed to) vs 'Whose laptop is this?' (determiner use).

exercises.question: ___ caravan were you staying in? (Correction of: Who's)
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Whose
'Whose' asks about possession or belonging. It can be used as a determiner ('Whose car?') or as a pronoun ('Whose is this?'). It replaces 'his/her/their + noun' in questions.

exercises.question: He asked us ___ car was parked in front of his house. (Correction of: who's)
exercises.explanation:
Answer: whose
In indirect questions, 'whose' functions as a possessive determiner: 'He asked whose car was parked there.' The word order in indirect questions is subject + verb (not inverted).

exercises.question: ___ going with you to Canada? (Correction of: Whose)
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both Who's and Who is
'Who's' is a contraction of 'who is'. 'Who is going with you?' can be contracted to 'Who's going with you?' Both 'who's' and 'who is' are correct. Note: 'whose' is the possessive form.
